claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claims.claim: Activation of >10 nociceptor cells was required to elicit rolling responses in a majority of larvae.
claims.source: Of note, prior studies demonstrated that sparse thermogenetic activation of nociceptors (<5 cells) yielded no significant increase in nocifensive rolling whereas activation of >10 cells was required to elicit rolling responses in a majority of larvae (Robertson et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claims.claim: Epidermal stimulation likely engages numerous C4da neurons to elicit behavioral responses.
claims.source: Hence, epidermal stimulation likely engages numerous C4da neurons to elicit these behavioral responses.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on prior work showing that multiple nociceptors must be activated to elicit rolling.

claims.claim: The epidermis is innervated by C3da, chordotonal (Cho) neurons, and proprioceptive C1da neurons in addition to C4da nociceptors.
claims.source: In addition to C4da nociceptors, the epidermis is innervated by a variety of other SSNs including mechanosensory C3da and chordotonal (Cho) neurons and proprioceptive C1da neurons.
claims.evidence: This is a statement of established anatomical knowledge about Drosophila sensory neurons.

claims.claim: Direct stimulation of C4da nociceptors principally elicited nocifensive behavioral outputs.
claims.source: Whereas direct stimulation of C4da nociceptors principally elicited nocifensive behavioral outputs, epidermal stimulation elicited an array of behaviors in addition to nocifensive responses, including freezing and hunching (Figure 2A and B, Figure 2—videos 1 and 2), behaviors associated with stimulation of C3da and Cho neurons (Zhang et al., 2013; Turner et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claims.claim: Epidermal stimulation elicited an array of behaviors in addition to nocifensive responses, including freezing and hunching.
claims.source: Whereas direct stimulation of C4da nociceptors principally elicited nocifensive behavioral outputs, epidermal stimulation elicited an array of behaviors in addition to nocifensive responses, including freezing and hunching (Figure 2A and B, Figure 2—videos 1 and 2), behaviors associated with stimulation of C3da and Cho neurons (Zhang et al., 2013; Turner et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claims.claim: Freezing and hunching behaviors are associated with stimulation of C3da and Cho neurons.
claims.source: Whereas direct stimulation of C4da nociceptors principally elicited nocifensive behavioral outputs, epidermal stimulation elicited an array of behaviors in addition to nocifensive responses, including freezing and hunching (Figure 2A and B, Figure 2—videos 1 and 2), behaviors associated with stimulation of C3da and Cho neurons (Zhang et al., 2013; Turner et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claims.claim: Epidermal cells may broadly modulate SSN activity in Drosophila.
claims.source: These data suggest that epidermal cells may broadly modulate SSN activity in Drosophila.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis inferred from the observation that epidermal stimulation elicits behaviors associated with multiple SSN types.

claims.claim: Only C4da neurons elicited rolling behavior when stimulated.
claims.source: Stimulation of C4da, C3da, and Cho neurons elicited distinct behavioral motifs: only C4da neurons elicited rolling behavior; stimulation of C3da and Cho neurons together elicited hunching, C-bending, and backing; stimulation of Cho neurons alone principally elicited hunching and freezing responses (Figure 2A–C and F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A–C and F.

claims.claim: Stimulation of C3da and Cho neurons together elicited hunching, C-bending, and backing.
claims.source: Stimulation of C4da, C3da, and Cho neurons elicited distinct behavioral motifs: only C4da neurons elicited rolling behavior; stimulation of C3da and Cho neurons together elicited hunching, C-bending, and backing; stimulation of Cho neurons alone principally elicited hunching and freezing responses (Figure 2A–C and F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A–C and F.

claims.claim: Stimulation of Cho neurons alone principally elicited hunching and freezing responses.
claims.source: Stimulation of C4da, C3da, and Cho neurons elicited distinct behavioral motifs: only C4da neurons elicited rolling behavior; stimulation of C3da and Cho neurons together elicited hunching, C-bending, and backing; stimulation of Cho neurons alone principally elicited hunching and freezing responses (Figure 2A–C and F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A–C and F.

claims.claim: Optogenetic epidermal stimulation elicited all behaviors observed with SSN stimulation, with nocifensive behaviors (c-bending, rolling) predominating initially, followed by non-nociceptive behaviors (backing, freezing).
claims.source: In contrast, optogenetic epidermal stimulation elicited all of these behaviors, with nocifensive behaviors (c-bending, rolling) predominating initially, followed by non-nociceptive behaviors (backing, freezing) (Figure 2D and F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and F.

claims.claim: Latency to rolling was significantly longer following epidermal stimulation compared to stimulation of C4da.
claims.source: First, although rapid, latency to rolling was significantly longer following epidermal stimulation compared to stimulation of C4da (Figure 2F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claims.claim: The duration of rolling, bending, and backing responses was significantly longer for epidermis versus SSN stimulation.
claims.source: Second, the duration of rolling, bending, and backing responses was significantly longer for epidermis versus SSN stimulation (Figure 2G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claims.claim: Backing and freezing behaviors persisted beyond the duration of the light stimulus for epidermis but not SSN stimulation.
claims.source: Third, backing and freezing behaviors persisted beyond the duration of the light stimulus for epidermis but not SSN stimulation (Figure 2H).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H.

claims.claim: Epidermal stimulation triggers more robust, varied, and prolonged behaviors compared to responses from direct stimulation of discrete SSN subtypes.
claims.source: In summary, we find that epidermal stimulation triggers more robust, varied, and prolonged behaviors compared to responses from direct stimulation of discrete SSN subtypes.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the behavioral comparison data.

claims.claim: Epidermal stimulation triggered rapid and robust calcium transients in nociceptive C4da neurons.
claims.source: We found that epidermal stimulation triggered rapid and robust calcium transients in nociceptive C4da neurons, responses that were not observed in the absence of ATR or in effector-only controls (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Epidermal stimulation evoked calcium transients in mechanosensory C3da and Cho neurons, and in proprioceptive C1da neurons.
claims.source: Epidermal stimulation likewise evoked calcium transients in mechanosensory C3da and Cho neurons, and in proprioceptive C1da neurons (Figure 3C–E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3C–E.

claims.claim: Epidermal stimulation can broadly modulate activity of larval SSNs.
claims.source: Hence, epidermal stimulation can broadly modulate activity of larval SSNs.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the calcium imaging data showing responses in multiple SSN types.

claims.claim: Inhibiting C4da or C3da+Cho neurotransmission significantly reduced the frequency and duration of epidermal-evoked rolling and backing behaviors, respectively.
claims.source: We found that inhibiting C4da or C3da+Cho neurotransmission significantly reduced the frequency and duration of epidermal-evoked rolling and backing behaviors, respectively (Figure 3F and G, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using tetanus toxin to block neurotransmitter release, shown in Figure 3F and G.

claims.claim: C4da and C3da/Cho neurons act downstream of epidermal cells to drive behaviors.
claims.source: These data suggest that C4da and C3da/Cho neurons act downstream of epidermal cells to drive behaviors.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the neurotransmitter release blocking experiments.

claims.claim: TnT expression in C4da neurons did not completely block epidermis-evoked nocifensive behaviors.
claims.source: We note that TnT expression in C4da neurons did not completely block epidermis-evoked nocifensive behaviors, and this likely reflects both incomplete C4da neuron silencing and epidermal activation of other SSNs that promote nociceptive outputs including C3da neurons, C2da neurons, and Cho neurons (Ohyama et al., 2015; Hu et al., 2017; Burgos et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data with an inference about the underlying mechanisms.

claims.claim: Silencing C4da or C3da/Cho neurons while stimulating epidermal cells led to an increase in the non-nocifensive behaviors hunching and freezing.
claims.source: Further, silencing C4da or C3da/Cho neurons while stimulating epidermal cells led to an increase in the non-nocifensive behaviors hunching and freezing (Figure 3F and G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F and G.

claims.claim: The nervous system prioritizes nocifensive behavioral outputs following epidermal stimulation.
claims.source: These results, along with the observation that rolling behaviors predominate the early behavioral responses to epidermal stimulation (Figure 2B), suggest that the nervous system prioritizes nocifensive behavioral outputs following epidermal stimulation.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis inferred from the behavioral data.

claims.claim: Epidermal cells and SSNs are functionally coupled.
claims.source: These data support a model in which epidermal cells and SSNs are functionally coupled.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the experimental data showing that epidermal stimulation activates SSNs and drives behaviors.

claims.claim: Simultaneous epidermal and C4da stimulation significantly enhanced the magnitude and duration of calcium responses in C4da axons.
claims.source: Simultaneous stimulation significantly enhanced the magnitude and duration of calcium responses in C4da axons (Figure 4A–D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4A–D.

claims.claim: Simultaneous epidermal cell and C4da neuron stimulation resulted in rolling in 100% of larvae.
claims.source: In this stimulation paradigm, simultaneous epidermal cell and C4da neuron stimulation resulted in rolling in 100% of larvae whereas selective stimulation of C4da neurons or epidermal cells induced rolling in only 63% or 18% of larvae, respectively (Figure 4E and F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4E and F.

claims.claim: Selective stimulation of C4da neurons induced rolling in 63% of larvae.
claims.source: In this stimulation paradigm, simultaneous epidermal cell and C4da neuron stimulation resulted in rolling in 100% of larvae whereas selective stimulation of C4da neurons or epidermal cells induced rolling in only 63% or 18% of larvae, respectively (Figure 4E and F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4E and F.

claims.claim: Selective stimulation of epidermal cells induced rolling in 18% of larvae.
claims.source: In this stimulation paradigm, simultaneous epidermal cell and C4da neuron stimulation resulted in rolling in 100% of larvae whereas selective stimulation of C4da neurons or epidermal cells induced rolling in only 63% or 18% of larvae, respectively (Figure 4E and F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4E and F.

claims.claim: Simultaneous stimulation elicited a significantly higher number of rolls among responders than stimulation of nociceptors or epidermal cells alone.
claims.source: Furthermore, simultaneous stimulation elicited a significantly higher number of rolls among responders than stimulation of nociceptors or epidermal cells alone (26.9 rolls for C4da+Epi, 4.9 for C4da, and 5.3 for Epi stimulation; Figure 4G and H).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4G and H.

claims.claim: Simultaneous stimulation significantly reduced the latency to the first roll.
claims.source: Likewise, simultaneous stimulation significantly reduced the latency to the first roll (Figure 4I) and increased the duration of rolling behaviors (Figure 4J).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4I.

claims.claim: Simultaneous stimulation increased the duration of rolling behaviors.
claims.source: Likewise, simultaneous stimulation significantly reduced the latency to the first roll (Figure 4I) and increased the duration of rolling behaviors (Figure 4J).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4J.

claims.claim: Concurrent epidermal stimulation significantly increased touch-evoked nocifensive responses, yielding a 91% or 49% increase in rolling responses to 20 mN or 50 mN von Frey stimulus, respectively.
claims.source: This concurrent epidermal stimulation significantly increased touch-evoked nocifensive responses, yielding a 91% or 49% increase in rolling responses to 20 mN or 50 mN von Frey stimulus, respectively (Figure 4K).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4K.

claims.claim: dTRPA1-mediated epidermal stimulation significantly sensitized larvae to a subsequent mechanical stimulus, increasing the roll probability more than twofold.
claims.source: Indeed, we found that dTRPA1-mediated epidermal stimulation significantly sensitized larvae to a subsequent mechanical stimulus, increasing the roll probability more than twofold.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4L.

claims.claim: dTRPA1-mediated stimulation of C4da neurons did not induce mechanical sensitization.
claims.source: In contrast, dTRPA1-mediated stimulation of C4da neurons did not induce mechanical sensitization, and we confirmed this result with two independent C4da neuron drivers (Figure 4L).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4L.

claims.claim: Activation of epidermal cells but not C4da nociceptors alone induces prolonged sensitization to noxious mechanical stimuli.
claims.source: Thus, activation of epidermal cells but not C4da nociceptors alone induces prolonged sensitization to noxious mechanical stimuli.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the behavioral data comparing epidermal and nociceptor stimulation.

claims.claim: Thermogenetic epidermal stimulation yielded persistent sensitization that recovered over a timescale of minutes (τ=337 s).
claims.source: Thermogenetic epidermal stimulation yielded persistent sensitization that recovered over a timescale of minutes (τ=337 s, Figure 4M and N).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4M and N.

claims.claim: The magnitude and duration of mechanical sensitization by thermogenetic epidermal stimulation was remarkably similar to sensitization evoked by a prior mechanical stimulus (63% roll probability in response to a second stimulus, τ=334 s).
claims.source: The magnitude and duration of mechanical sensitization by thermogenetic epidermal stimulation was remarkably similar to sensitization evoked by a prior mechanical stimulus (63% roll probability in response to a second stimulus, τ=334 s, Figure 4N, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4N and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Epidermal cells are mechanosensitive cells that signal to SSNs to drive acute nocifensive behaviors and prolong mechanical sensitization.
claims.source: Altogether our data support a model whereby epidermal cells are mechanosensitive cells that signal to SSNs to drive acute nocifensive behaviors and prolong mechanical sensitization.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the experimental data.

claims.claim: Vertebrate epidermal cells directly respond to mechanical stimuli.
claims.source: Prior studies have shown that vertebrate epidermal cells directly respond to mechanical stimuli (Koizumi et al., 2004; Haeberle et al., 2008; Tsutsumi et al., 2009; Ranade et al., 2014; Woo et al., 2014; Moehring et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claims.claim: Radial stretch elicits calcium responses in epidermal cells in a dose-dependent manner.
claims.source: We found that radial stretch elicits calcium responses in epidermal cells in a dose-dependent manner.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data from dissociated epidermal cells shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: A low 0.5% stretch activated 18% of cells and a subsequent 1% stretch recruited an additional 10% of stretch-responding cells.
claims.source: For example, a low 0.5% stretch activated 18% of cells and a subsequent 1% stretch recruited an additional 10% of stretch-responding cells (Figure 5B–D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5B–D.

claims.claim: 51% of epidermal cells displayed stretch sensitivity.
claims.source: Overall, 51% of epidermal cells displayed stretch sensitivity (Figure 5C and D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5C and D.

claims.claim: 43% of epidermal cells responded to hypoosmotic challenge.
claims.source: We also found that 43% of epidermal cells responded to hypoosmotic challenge and 35% responded to laminar flow; 19% of epidermal cells responded to both hypoosmotic challenge and laminar flow (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: 35% of epidermal cells responded to laminar flow.
claims.source: We also found that 43% of epidermal cells responded to hypoosmotic challenge and 35% responded to laminar flow; 19% of epidermal cells responded to both hypoosmotic challenge and laminar flow (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: 19% of epidermal cells responded to both hypoosmotic challenge and laminar flow.
claims.source: We also found that 43% of epidermal cells responded to hypoosmotic challenge and 35% responded to laminar flow; 19% of epidermal cells responded to both hypoosmotic challenge and laminar flow (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: 50% of epidermal cells exhibited a robust calcium transient in response to a 25 μm membrane displacement using a glass probe.
claims.source: We found that 50% of epidermal cells exhibited a robust calcium transient in response to a 25 μm membrane displacement using a glass probe (Figure 5E–G, Figure 5—figure supplement 1G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5E–G.

claims.claim: Drosophila larval epidermal cells are intrinsically mechanosensitive.
claims.source: Altogether, these results indicate that Drosophila larval epidermal cells are intrinsically mechanosensitive.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the calcium imaging data from dissociated and semi-intact preparations.

claims.claim: RNA-seq analysis of acutely dissociated epidermal cells revealed expression of more than 20 cation channels, including the mechanosensitive ion channels Piezo, TMEM63, and TMCO.
claims.source: RNA-seq analysis of acutely dissociated epidermal cells revealed expression of more than 20 cation channels, including the mechanosensitive ion channels Piezo, TMEM63, and TMCO (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Orai blocked mechanically evoked nociceptive sensitization without impacting behavioral responses to the first stimulus.
claims.source: Our behavioral screen identified one channel, Orai, the sole Drosophila pore-forming subunit of the Ca2+ release-activated Ca2+ (CRAC) channel (Feske et al., 2006), that blocked mechanically evoked nociceptive sensitization without impacting behavioral responses to the first stimulus (Figure 6A and B, Figure 6—figure supplement 2) or altering nociceptor morphogenesis (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claims.claim: Orai is the sole Drosophila pore-forming subunit of the Ca2+ release-activated Ca2+ (CRAC) channel.
claims.source: Our behavioral screen identified one channel, Orai, the sole Drosophila pore-forming subunit of the Ca2+ release-activated Ca2+ (CRAC) channel (Feske et al., 2006), that blocked mechanically evoked nociceptive sensitization without impacting behavioral responses to the first stimulus (Figure 6A and B, Figure 6—figure supplement 2) or altering nociceptor morphogenesis (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claims.claim: Task6 is an orthologue of stretch-sensitive two-pore potassium channels.
claims.source: Interestingly, our screen uncovered an epidermal role for Task6, an orthologue of stretch-sensitive two-pore potassium channels (Fink et al., 1996), in mechanonociception, as Task6 RNAi increased nocifensive rolling responses to the initial mechanical stimulus (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claims.claim: Task6 RNAi increased nocifensive rolling responses to the initial mechanical stimulus.
claims.source: Interestingly, our screen uncovered an epidermal role for Task6, an orthologue of stretch-sensitive two-pore potassium channels (Fink et al., 1996), in mechanonociception, as Task6 RNAi increased nocifensive rolling responses to the initial mechanical stimulus (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: Drosophila epidermal cells display TG-induced calcium release from stores in the absence of extracellular calcium, followed by calcium influx upon re-addition of extracellular calcium.
claims.source: Indeed, Drosophila epidermal cells displayed TG-induced calcium release from stores in the absence of extracellular calcium, followed by calcium influx upon re-addition of extracellular calcium (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: Calcium influx was significantly inhibited by the addition of low nanomolar lanthanum.
claims.source: Calcium influx was significantly inhibited by the addition of low nanomolar lanthanum, consistent with the high sensitivity of Orai channels to lanthanides (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C.

claims.claim: Store-operated calcium entry (SOCE) response was significantly reduced by epidermis-specific Stim or Orai RNAi knockdown.
claims.source: This characteristic store-operated calcium entry (SOCE) response was significantly reduced by epidermis-specific Stim or Orai RNAi knockdown (Figure 6—figure supplement 2D–F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2D–F.

claims.claim: Radial stretch in the absence of extracellular calcium induced calcium release from intracellular stores, as well as calcium influx upon re-addition of extracellular calcium.
claims.source: Consistent with a key role for SOCE in mechanotransduction, we found that radial stretch in the absence of extracellular calcium induced calcium release from intracellular stores, as well as calcium influx upon re-addition of extracellular calcium.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: Mechanically evoked responses in epidermal cells involve both ER calcium release and SOCE.
claims.source: These data show that mechanically evoked responses in epidermal cells involve both ER calcium release and SOCE.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the calcium imaging data.

claims.claim: In 69% of cells, calcium due to store release exceeded that of calcium re-entry.
claims.source: While both store release and calcium influx constitute the calcium response to stretch, in 69% of cells, calcium due to store release exceeded that of calcium re-entry (Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: Depletion of intracellular stores reduced the number of stretch-sensitive cells by 61%.
claims.source: Consistent with this observation, depletion of intracellular stores and inhibition of calcium influx reduced the number of stretch-sensitve cells by 61% (stretch non-responsive cells in WT = 49% vs. store depleted = 80%) and 30% (stretch non-responsive cells in WT = 49% vs. La3+ = 64%; Figure 6F and G), respectively.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 6F and G.

claims.claim: Inhibition of calcium influx reduced the number of stretch-sensitive cells by 30%.
claims.source: Consistent with this observation, depletion of intracellular stores and inhibition of calcium influx reduced the number of stretch-sensitve cells by 61% (stretch non-responsive cells in WT = 49% vs. store depleted = 80%) and 30% (stretch non-responsive cells in WT = 49% vs. La3+ = 64%; Figure 6F and G), respectively.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 6F and G.

claims.claim: RNAi knockdown of either Stim or Orai significantly reduced the fraction of stretch-responsive epidermal cells.
claims.source: RNAi knockdown of either Stim or Orai significantly reduced the fraction of stretch-responsive epidermal cells (RNAi control = 48%, Stim RNAi = 22%, Orai RNAi = 24%; Figure 6H and I), with Stim or Orai RNAi preferentially attenuating stretch evoked responses to larger magnitude stretch stimuli.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 6H and I.

claims.claim: Stim or Orai RNAi preferentially attenuated stretch evoked responses to larger magnitude stretch stimuli.
claims.source: RNAi knockdown of either Stim or Orai significantly reduced the fraction of stretch-responsive epidermal cells (RNAi control = 48%, Stim RNAi = 22%, Orai RNAi = 24%; Figure 6H and I), with Stim or Orai RNAi preferentially attenuating stretch evoked responses to larger magnitude stretch stimuli.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the calcium imaging data.

claims.claim: Human keratinocytes display dose-dependent stretch evoked calcium responses.
claims.source: We also found that human keratinocytes display dose-dependent stretch evoked calcium responses, though they respond to higher magnitudes of stretch than Drosophila epidermal cells (Figure 6J).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 6J.

claims.claim: Human keratinocytes respond to higher magnitudes of stretch than Drosophila epidermal cells.
claims.source: We also found that human keratinocytes display dose-dependent stretch evoked calcium responses, though they respond to higher magnitudes of stretch than Drosophila epidermal cells (Figure 6J).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison based on calcium imaging data shown in Figure 6J.

claims.claim: Both ER calcium release and SOCE constitute the mechanically evoked calcium responses in human keratinocytes.
claims.source: Like Drosophila epidermal cells, both ER calcium release and SOCE constitute the mechanically evoked calcium responses in human keratinocytes (Figure 6K).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 6K.

claims.claim: Hyperpolarizing epidermal cells with the light-activated anion channelrhodopsin GtACR1 increased behavioral responses to mechanical stimuli.
claims.source: Indeed, we found that hyperpolarizing epidermal cells with the light-activated anion channelrhodopsin GtACR1 (Mohammad et al., 2017) increased behavioral responses to mechanical stimuli (Figure 6L).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6L.

claims.claim: Overexpressing Stim in epidermal cells significantly enhanced nocifensive behavioral responses to mechanical stimuli.
claims.source: In addition, overexpressing Stim in epidermal cells significantly enhanced nocifensive behavioral responses to mechanical stimuli (Figure 6M).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6M.

claims.claim: Stim/Orai-mediated calcium entry contributes to exocytosis in a variety of cell types, including neurons and immune cells.
claims.source: Stim/Orai-mediated calcium entry contributes to exocytosis in a variety of cell types, including neurons and immune cells (Pores-Fernando and Zweifach, 2009; Ashmole et al., 2012; Maneshi et al., 2020; Chanaday et al., 2021; Ramesh et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claims.claim: Larvae expressing shits in epidermal cells exhibited significant attenuation of mechanically evoked nociceptive sensitization following preincubation at the non-permissive temperature.
claims.source: In this paradigm, larvae expressing shits in epidermal cells, but not control larvae, exhibited significant attenuation of mechanically evoked nociceptive sensitization following preincubation at the non-permissive temperature (Figure 6N).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6N.

claims.claim: Both genotypes exhibited comparable responses to a mechanical stimulus at the permissive temperature (25°C) and to the first mechanical stimulus following preincubation at the non-permissive temperature (30°C).
claims.source: In contrast, both genotypes exhibited comparable responses to a mechanical stimulus at the permissive temperature (25°C) and to the first mechanical stimulus following preincubation at the non-permissive temperature (30°C).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the behavioral data shown in Figure 6N.

claims.claim: Mechanical stimuli induce calcium influx and vesicular release from epidermal cells, which in turn activates nociceptors to induce acute nocifensive behaviors and prolonged sensitization.
claims.source: Taken together, these results are consistent with a model in which mechanical stimuli induce calcium influx and vesicular release from epidermal cells, which in turn activates nociceptors to induce acute nocifensive behaviors and prolonged sensitization (Figure 6O).
claims.evidence: This is a model inferred from the experimental data.

claims.claim: Epidermal cells express a large repertoire of genes involved in vesicular release as well as several neuropeptide genes.
claims.source: Although our RNA-seq analysis of epidermal cells did not reveal expression of neurotransmitter biosynthesis genes, epidermal cells express a large repertoire of genes involved in vesicular release as well as several neuropeptide genes, providing an entry point to defining the molecules involved in epidermis-SSN communication (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: RNA-seq analysis of epidermal cells did not reveal expression of neurotransmitter biosynthesis genes.
claims.source: Although our RNA-seq analysis of epidermal cells did not reveal expression of neurotransmitter biosynthesis genes, epidermal cells express a large repertoire of genes involved in vesicular release as well as several neuropeptide genes, providing an entry point to defining the molecules involved in epidermis-SSN communication (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: Drosophila epidermal cells play an essential role in escape responses to noxious mechanical stimuli.
claims.source: In this study, we have shown an essential role for Drosophila epidermal cells in escape responses to noxious mechanical stimuli.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experimental data.

claims.claim: Activation of epidermal cells acutely activates SSNs to induce an array of behavioral outputs and mechanical sensitization.
claims.source: Activation of epidermal cells acutely activates SSNs to induce an array of behavioral outputs and mechanical sensitization.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experimental data.

claims.claim: Epidermal potentiation persists for minutes to promote a prolonged, but reversible, mechanical hypersensitivity that may protect from further insult.
claims.source: This epidermal potentiation persists for minutes to promote a prolonged, but reversible, mechanical hypersensitivity that may protect from further insult.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the behavioral data with a speculative component about the protective function.

claims.claim: Neuropathic thermal and mechanical hypersensitivity in Drosophila are induced by tissue damage and chemotherapeutic agents, respectively, emerge on a timescale of hours and are long-lasting.
claims.source: This is distinct from previously described forms of neuropathic thermal and mechanical hypersensitivity in Drosophila which are induced by tissue damage and chemotherapeutic agents, respectively, emerge on a timescale of hours and are long-lasting (Babcock et al., 2009; Boiko et al., 2017; Khuong et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claims.claim: A variety of inflammatory mediators have been shown to activate TRPA1 in neurons to promote mechanical hypersensitivity in the mammalian somatosensory system.
claims.source: In the mammalian somatosensory system, a variety of inflammatory mediators have been shown to activate TRPA1 in neurons to promote mechanical hypersensitivity (Bautista et al., 2006); however, the molecular force transducers that mediate mechanical pain remain unknown.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claims.claim: The molecular force transducers that mediate mechanical pain remain unknown in the mammalian somatosensory system.
claims.source: In the mammalian somatosensory system, a variety of inflammatory mediators have been shown to activate TRPA1 in neurons to promote mechanical hypersensitivity (Bautista et al., 2006); however, the molecular force transducers that mediate mechanical pain remain unknown.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claims.claim: Ppk1/Ppk26, Piezo, and Trpa1 are key transducers of mechanonociception in the Drosophila somatosensory system.

results.result: Optogenetic stimulation of Drosophila epidermal cells elicits nocifensive behaviors including rolling and c-bending in a majority of larvae (73-75%), comparable to direct nociceptor stimulation (100%). This response is specific to epidermal cells among non-neuronal body wall cell types and is observed across multiple epidermal GAL4 drivers.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C4, C23, C24, C28, C29, C31, C32, and C33 provide converging evidence from optogenetic and thermogenetic experiments using multiple independent GAL4 drivers. The behavioral responses are well-documented with appropriate controls (ATR+/-, GAL80 silencing of neuronal expression), and the specificity is demonstrated by comparison with other body wall cell types (C26, C27, C28).

results.result: Epidermal stimulation elicits a broader behavioral repertoire than direct stimulation of individual sensory neuron subtypes, including both nocifensive (rolling, c-bending) and non-nocifensive (freezing, hunching, backing) behaviors. Epidermis-evoked behaviors show longer latency, duration, and persistence beyond stimulus offset compared to direct neuronal stimulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C49 are supported by systematic behavioral comparisons using high-resolution video tracking with appropriate controls. The temporal dynamics and behavioral diversity are quantified across multiple neuron types (C4da, C3da, Cho) and compared to epidermal stimulation, providing strong evidence for the broader and more prolonged nature of epidermis-evoked responses.

results.result: Epidermal stimulation activates multiple classes of somatosensory neurons (C4da, C3da, Cho, C1da) as measured by calcium imaging, and blocking neurotransmitter release from these neurons reduces epidermis-evoked behaviors, demonstrating functional coupling between epidermal cells and sensory neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C54 and C58 are supported by calcium imaging experiments showing neuronal activation (with appropriate ATR+/- and effector-only controls) and tetanus toxin experiments demonstrating requirement for neuronal output. The convergence of imaging and genetic silencing data provides strong evidence for epidermis-neuron functional coupling.

results.result: Simultaneous epidermal and nociceptor stimulation enhances nociceptive responses compared to stimulation of either cell type alone, increasing calcium response magnitude/duration in C4da neurons, rolling probability (100% vs 63% or 18%), number of rolls (26.9 vs 4.9 or 5.3), and reducing latency. Concurrent epidermal stimulation also enhances mechanical stimulus-evoked responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C66 are supported by both calcium imaging and behavioral data showing synergistic effects of combined stimulation. The quantitative measurements of calcium dynamics, rolling probability, roll number, latency, and duration provide robust evidence for epidermal potentiation of nociceptive responses. Statistical significance is reported for key comparisons.

results.result: Thermogenetic epidermal stimulation induces prolonged mechanical sensitization lasting several minutes (τ=337 s), increasing roll probability more than twofold to subsequent mechanical stimuli. This sensitization is specific to epidermal stimulation and not observed with direct nociceptor stimulation, and is comparable in magnitude and duration to sensitization from prior mechanical stimuli.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C71 are supported by behavioral experiments using dTRPA1-mediated stimulation with appropriate controls (temperature, genotype). The time course of sensitization is quantified with exponential decay fitting, and the specificity is demonstrated by comparison with nociceptor stimulation using two independent C4da drivers. The similarity to mechanical stimulus-evoked sensitization strengthens the physiological relevance.

results.result: Drosophila larval epidermal cells are intrinsically mechanosensitive, responding to radial stretch (51% of cells), hypoosmotic challenge (43%), laminar flow (35%), and mechanical poking (50%) with calcium transients in both dissociated cell and semi-intact preparations.
results.evaluation: Claims C5 and C74-C81 are supported by calcium imaging experiments in multiple preparations (dissociated cells, body wall fillets) using different mechanical stimuli. The dose-dependent responses to stretch and the quantification of responding cell fractions provide strong evidence for intrinsic mechanosensitivity. The use of multiple stimulus modalities strengthens the conclusion.

results.result: Mechanically evoked calcium responses in epidermal cells require the store-operated calcium channel Orai and its activator Stim. Mechanical stretch induces both ER calcium release and SOCE, with RNAi knockdown of Stim or Orai reducing stretch-responsive cells from 48% to 22-24%. Orai knockdown blocks mechanical sensitization without affecting acute nociceptive responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C6 and C83-C96 are supported by multiple lines of evidence: behavioral screen identifying Orai (C83), pharmacological inhibition with lanthanum (C88), RNAi knockdown experiments (C89, C95), and calcium imaging in zero-calcium conditions demonstrating SOCE (C87, C90). The convergence of genetic, pharmacological, and imaging approaches provides strong support for the Stim/Orai mechanism.

results.result: Human keratinocytes display dose-dependent stretch-evoked calcium responses involving both ER calcium release and SOCE, similar to Drosophila epidermal cells but responding to higher stretch magnitudes.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C99 are supported by calcium imaging experiments in HaCaT cells using radial stretch and calcium re-addition protocols. The demonstration of similar mechanisms in human cells strengthens the translational relevance of the findings, though the higher stretch threshold suggests species-specific differences in mechanosensitivity.

results.result: Manipulations that increase Orai channel activity—hyperpolarizing epidermal cells with GtACR1 or overexpressing Stim—enhance behavioral responses to mechanical stimuli, consistent with Orai's biophysical properties (inward rectification and cooperative Stim activation).
results.evaluation: Claims C100 and C101 are supported by behavioral experiments showing increased mechanical responses with GtACR1-mediated hyperpolarization and Stim overexpression. These gain-of-function experiments complement the loss-of-function RNAi data and are consistent with known Orai channel properties, providing additional support for the Stim/Orai mechanism.

results.result: Mechanical sensitization requires dynamin-dependent vesicular release from epidermal cells. Temperature-sensitive dynamin (shibirets) expression in epidermis attenuates mechanically evoked sensitization at non-permissive temperature without affecting acute responses, supporting a model where mechanical stimuli induce calcium influx and vesicular release from epidermal cells to activate nociceptors.
results.evaluation: Claims C103, C104, C105, and C132 are supported by behavioral experiments using shibirets at permissive and non-permissive temperatures with appropriate controls. The selective effect on sensitization without affecting acute responses provides strong evidence for vesicular release in the sensitization mechanism. However, the specific mediators released remain unidentified (C133), limiting mechanistic understanding.

results.result: RNA-seq analysis of epidermal cells reveals expression of genes involved in vesicular release and neuropeptide genes, but not classical neurotransmitter biosynthesis genes, providing candidate molecules for epidermis-SSN communication.
results.evaluation: Claims C106 and C107 are supported by RNA-seq data from dissociated epidermal cells. The absence of neurotransmitter biosynthesis genes but presence of vesicular release machinery and neuropeptides is consistent with the shibirets results and suggests non-classical signaling mechanisms. However, functional validation of specific candidates is not provided.

results.result: RNA-seq analysis of epidermal cells identified expression of more than 20 cation channels including mechanosensitive channels Piezo, TMEM63, and TMCO.
results.evaluation: Claim C82 is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1. The expression data provides a foundation for the ion channel screen, though the functional roles of most channels beyond Orai remain unexplored in this study.

results.result: RNAi knockdown of Task6, an orthologue of stretch-sensitive two-pore potassium channels, increased nocifensive rolling responses to the initial mechanical stimulus, suggesting a role in modulating acute mechanonociception.
results.evaluation: Claim C86 is supported by behavioral data from the RNAi screen shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B. The increased response to initial stimulus (opposite to Orai's effect on sensitization) suggests Task6 may dampen acute responses, though the mechanism is not explored further.

results.result: Optogenetic stimulation of epidermal cells does not significantly alter nociceptor morphogenesis, as assessed by dendrite length and branch point analysis.
results.evaluation: Claim C25 is supported by morphometric analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4. This control experiment rules out developmental effects of epidermal manipulations on nociceptor structure, strengthening the interpretation that behavioral effects are due to functional signaling rather than morphological changes.

results.result: Incomplete blocking of epidermis-evoked nocifensive behaviors by C4da neuron silencing likely reflects both incomplete silencing and activation of other SSNs (C3da, C2da, Cho) that contribute to nociceptive outputs. Silencing C4da or C3da/Cho neurons increases non-nocifensive behaviors, suggesting the nervous system prioritizes nocifensive outputs following epidermal stimulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C57 involve interpretations of incomplete phenotypes. While the observation of incomplete blocking (C55) and increased non-nocifensive behaviors (C56) is supported by data in Figure 3F-G, the inference about nervous system prioritization (C57) is speculative. The incomplete blocking could reflect technical limitations (incomplete TnT expression) or biological complexity (multiple parallel pathways), and distinguishing these requires additional experiments.

results.result: Epidermal cells are key determinants of nociceptive sensitivity and sensitization, acting as primary sensors of noxious stimuli that tune nociceptor output and drive protective behaviors. This mechanism selectively regulates mechanical sensitization without impacting acute nociception.
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C10, C72, C108, C109, C110, and C119 represent high-level conclusions synthesizing the experimental findings. These are well-supported by the convergence of optogenetic/thermogenetic stimulation, calcium imaging, behavioral sensitization, and mechanistic (Stim/Orai, vesicular release) data. The characterization as 'primary sensors' is justified by the intrinsic mechanosensitivity data, and the selective effect on sensitization vs. acute responses is demonstrated by the Orai knockdown experiments.

results.result: This work establishes a novel role for mechanically evoked Stim/Orai calcium signaling in epidermal cells driving nociceptor modulation and mechanical hypersensitivity, highlighting Stim/Orai signaling as a new avenue for understanding mechanical pain.
results.evaluation: Claims C116, C120, and C154 represent summary statements about the novelty and significance of the findings. These are supported by the comprehensive experimental evidence demonstrating the Stim/Orai mechanism in both Drosophila and human epidermal cells, and the functional link to nociceptive sensitization. The claim of novelty is supported by C121 (Orai not previously shown to be mechanosensitive).

results.result: Stim/Orai signaling may represent a conserved pathway for mechanotransduction in non-neuronal cells, based on similar SOCE responses to mechanical stimulation in Drosophila epidermal cells, human keratinocytes, human mesenchymal stem cells, and mouse enteroendocrine cells.
results.evaluation: Claim C123 is a hypothesis based on the current findings (C97-C99, C116) and prior published work (C122). While the demonstration of SOCE in both Drosophila and human epidermal cells supports conservation, the claim of a 'conserved pathway' requires more extensive comparative analysis across species and cell types. The cited prior work provides some support, but functional conservation of the mechanism (not just SOCE occurrence) needs further validation.

results.result: Epidermal stimulation likely engages numerous C4da neurons to elicit behavioral responses, based on prior work showing that activation of >10 nociceptors is required for rolling in a majority of larvae.
results.evaluation: Claim C36 is a reasonable inference based on prior published work (C34, C35) showing the threshold for nociceptor-evoked rolling. The calcium imaging data (C50) showing C4da activation and the robust behavioral responses (C24, C32) support this interpretation, though direct quantification of the number of activated neurons is not provided.

results.result: Epidermal cells may broadly modulate SSN activity in Drosophila, based on the observation that epidermal stimulation elicits behaviors associated with multiple SSN types (C3da, Cho neurons).
results.evaluation: Claim C41 is supported by the behavioral data (C39, C40) and calcium imaging showing activation of multiple SSN types (C51). However, this is presented as a hypothesis ('may') and the mechanisms of differential SSN activation and whether all SSNs are activated simultaneously or sequentially remain unclear.

results.result: The output of epidermal cells is likely dependent on stimulus intensity, based on the dose-dependent calcium responses to radial stretch.
results.evaluation: Claim C136 is a reasonable inference from the dose-dependent stretch responses (C74, C75, C135). However, this remains a hypothesis as the relationship between stimulus intensity, epidermal calcium responses, and behavioral output is not directly tested. Experiments varying mechanical stimulus intensity while measuring both epidermal and neuronal responses would strengthen this claim.

results.result: Epidermal stimulation evokes calcium responses from SSNs not ensheathed by epidermal cells (C1da, Cho neurons), suggesting epidermal sheaths are unlikely to play an essential function in epidermis-SSN functional coupling.
results.evaluation: Claims C141 and C142 are supported by the calcium imaging data showing responses in C1da and Cho neurons (C51). This observation argues against an absolute requirement for ensheathment in epidermis-SSN signaling. However, the conclusion that sheaths are 'unlikely to play an essential function' may be too strong—sheaths could still modulate signaling efficiency or specificity without being absolutely required.

results.result: Ensheathment may facilitate nociceptor activation by increasing vesicular exchange efficiency or modulating activity through enhanced ionic coupling to epidermal cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C143 and C144 are speculative hypotheses about potential functions of ensheathment. While these are reasonable possibilities given the vesicular release data (C103-C105) and the known existence of ensheathment (C137), no experimental evidence is provided to test these specific mechanisms. These represent future research directions rather than supported conclusions.

results.result: Background claims establishing prior knowledge about somatosensory systems, nociception, epidermal cell functions, and relevant molecular mechanisms in both Drosophila and mammalian systems.
results.evaluation: These claims (C1, C2, C11-C22, C30, C34, C35, C37, C40, C73, C84, C85, C102, C111-C115, C117, C121, C122, C124-C129, C137, C139, C140, C145-C151) represent established knowledge from prior published work, supported by appropriate citations. They provide context for the current study and are generally accurate representations of the cited literature.

results.result: Several key mechanistic questions remain unresolved, including: whether deregulation of epidermis-evoked sensitization contributes to pathological pain, the identity of mediators released by epidermal cells, whether different SSN types use distinct coupling mechanisms, whether growth factor signaling can yield rapid sensitization, and the nature of neuronal plasticity underlying mechanical sensitization.
results.evaluation: Claims C118, C133, C134, C152, and C153 explicitly acknowledge limitations and future research directions. These are appropriately presented as open questions rather than conclusions, demonstrating scientific rigor in distinguishing what has been established from what remains to be determined.

results.result: Optogenetic stimulation of Drosophila epidermal cells elicits nocifensive behaviors including rolling and c-bending in a majority of larvae (73%), as well as non-nociceptive behaviors like freezing and hunching. Epidermal stimulation triggers more robust, varied, and prolonged behaviors compared to direct stimulation of discrete sensory neuron subtypes.
results.evaluation: All three reviewers affirm this finding. Reviewer 1 states the experiments 'support the authors' main claim that epidermal cells are mechanosensitive' and that 'epidermal cells activate nociceptive sensory neurons...and thereby prolong escape rolling.' Reviewer 2 notes 'compelling evidence that stimulation of epidermal cells...results in the stimulation of sensory neurons that evoke a variety of behavioral responses.' The editor describes the evidence as 'convincing' and states it 'strongly implicates activation of epidermal cells...in the activation of nociceptive neurons.'

results.result: Epidermal stimulation triggers rapid calcium transients in multiple types of somatosensory neurons including nociceptive C4da neurons, mechanosensory C3da and Cho neurons, and proprioceptive C1da neurons, demonstrating functional coupling between epidermal cells and SSNs.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these calcium imaging findings without challenge. Reviewer 2 specifically notes 'behavioral studies are complemented by sophisticated optogenetics and imaging studies' as a strength. Reviewer 1 confirms the experiments are 'logical and complementary' and support the main claims. No reviewer questions the calcium imaging data or interpretation.

results.result: Inhibiting neurotransmission from C4da or C3da/Cho neurons using tetanus toxin significantly reduced epidermal-evoked rolling and backing behaviors, demonstrating that neuronal output is required for epidermis-evoked behaviors.
results.evaluation: This result is accepted by reviewers as part of the overall evidence for epidermis-neuron coupling. Reviewer 1 states the experiments 'support the authors' main claim' and are 'logical and complementary.' No reviewer challenges the tetanus toxin experiments or their interpretation. The genetic analyses are noted as 'thorough with appropriate consideration to potential confounds' by Reviewer 2.

results.result: Simultaneous stimulation of epidermal cells and C4da neurons significantly enhances calcium responses in nociceptors and behavioral outputs compared to stimulation of either cell type alone, with 100% of larvae rolling versus 63% (C4da alone) or 18% (epidermis alone).
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these findings. Reviewer 1 confirms the experiments 'support the authors' main claim' about epidermal cell mechanosensitivity and nociceptor activation. The editor states the evidence is 'convincing' for activation of epidermal cells in nociceptive neuron activation. No concerns are raised about the simultaneous stimulation experiments.

results.result: Epidermal cell stimulation promotes prolonged mechanical hypersensitivity lasting several minutes (τ=337 s), significantly sensitizing larvae to subsequent mechanical stimuli. This sensitization is specific to epidermal activation, as C4da neuron stimulation alone does not induce mechanical sensitization.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this finding as a key result. Reviewer 1 states the experiments support the claim that 'epidermal cells activate nociceptive sensory neurons...and thereby prolong escape rolling evoked by mechanical noxious stimulation.' Reviewer 2 notes the study 'represents a significant advance in our understanding of mechanosensation.' The editor confirms the evidence 'strongly implicates' epidermal cells in nociceptive neuron activation.

results.result: Drosophila larval epidermal cells are intrinsically mechanosensitive, with 51% of dissociated epidermal cells displaying stretch sensitivity in a dose-dependent manner. Mechanical stimulation with radial stretch or glass probe displacement elicits calcium responses in epidermal cells.
results.evaluation: All reviewers affirm this finding. Reviewer 1 explicitly states the experiments 'support the authors' main claim that epidermal cells are mechanosensitive and that epidermal mechanically evoked calcium responses require the stored-operated calcium channel Orai.' Reviewer 2 notes 'the authors demonstrate that epidermal cells are inherently mechanoresponsive.' The editor confirms the evidence is 'convincing' for this claim.

results.result: Epidermal mechanically evoked calcium responses require the store-operated calcium channel Orai and its activator Stim. RNAi knockdown of Stim or Orai significantly reduced stretch-responsive epidermal cells and blocked mechanically evoked nociceptive sensitization without impacting acute behavioral responses.
results.evaluation: Reviewers strongly support this finding. Reviewer 1 states experiments 'support the authors' main claim that...epidermal mechanically evoked calcium responses require the stored-operated calcium channel Orai.' Reviewer 2 identifies 'identification of roles for store-operated calcium entry is intriguing' as a key strength. The editor confirms evidence 'strongly implicates...store-operated calcium entry in the activation of nociceptive neurons.' This is treated as a novel and significant discovery.

results.result: Mechanically evoked responses in epidermal cells involve both ER calcium release and store-operated calcium entry (SOCE). In 69% of cells, calcium from store release exceeded calcium re-entry. Depletion of intracellular stores reduced stretch-sensitive cells by 61%, while inhibition of calcium influx reduced them by 30%.
results.evaluation: While reviewers accept the role of SOCE, Reviewer 2 raises conceptual concerns: 'The involvement of store-operated calcium entry implicates ER calcium store release. Whether mechanical stimulation evokes ER calcium release in epidermal cells and how this might come about...remains unaddressed.' This indicates the mechanism linking mechanical stimulation to ER calcium release is not fully resolved, though the data showing both components contribute is accepted.

results.result: Human keratinocytes display dose-dependent stretch-evoked calcium responses involving both ER calcium release and SOCE, similar to Drosophila epidermal cells, though they respond to higher magnitudes of stretch.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 notes 'conservation of these pathways in vertebrates raise the possibility that the described axis is also functional in vertebrates' as a strength. No reviewer challenges the human keratinocyte data. The conservation across species is treated as supporting the broader significance of the findings.

results.result: Hyperpolarizing epidermal cells with GtACR1 increased behavioral responses to mechanical stimuli, and overexpressing Stim in epidermal cells significantly enhanced nocifensive behavioral responses to mechanical stimuli.
results.evaluation: These gain-of-function experiments are accepted as part of the overall evidence for Stim/Orai function. Reviewer 2 notes 'the genetic analyses presented in the paper are thorough with appropriate consideration to potential confounds.' No specific concerns are raised about these manipulations.

results.result: Blocking dynamin-dependent vesicle release from epidermal cells using temperature-sensitive shibire significantly attenuated mechanically evoked nociceptive sensitization without affecting responses to the first mechanical stimulus, providing a link between Stim/Orai signaling and neuronal activity.
results.evaluation: While the data is accepted, Reviewer 2 raises a conceptual concern: 'On a related note, the kinetics of store-operated calcium entry is very distinct from that required for SV release. The link between SOC and epidermal cells-neuron transmission is not reconciled.' This indicates uncertainty about how SOCE mechanistically drives vesicular release, though the experimental observation itself is not challenged.

results.result: The authors propose a model in which mechanical stimuli induce calcium influx and vesicular release from epidermal cells, which activates nociceptors to induce acute nocifensive behaviors and prolonged sensitization. Epidermal cells are key determinants of nociceptive sensitivity and sensitization, acting as primary sensors of noxious stimuli.
results.evaluation: The overall model is accepted by reviewers. The editor states 'This is important work and provides a significant advance in our understanding of mechanosensation in the epidermis.' Reviewer 2 notes 'The study represents a significant advance in our understanding of mechanosensation.' While mechanistic details remain to be resolved (as noted in other results), the core model is supported.

results.result: Optogenetic or thermogenetic stimulation of epidermal cells does not significantly alter nociceptor morphogenesis, and GAL80 transgenes that silence sparse VNC expression have no effect on rolling frequency.
results.evaluation: These control experiments are accepted without challenge. Reviewer 2 notes 'the genetic analyses presented in the paper are thorough with appropriate consideration to potential confounds' as a strength. These controls address potential developmental or off-target effects.

results.result: RNA-seq analysis of epidermal cells revealed expression of more than 20 cation channels including mechanosensitive channels (Piezo, TMEM63, TMCO), genes involved in vesicular release, and several neuropeptide genes, but did not reveal expression of neurotransmitter biosynthesis genes.
results.evaluation: This descriptive RNA-seq data is accepted without challenge. It provides supporting molecular evidence for the functional findings. Reviewer 2 notes the genetic analyses are thorough, which would encompass this molecular characterization.

comparisons.comparison: Both strongly support that epidermal cell stimulation activates nociceptive sensory neurons and evokes behavioral responses. OpenEval emphasizes optogenetic/thermogenetic evidence with multiple GAL4 drivers (C3, C4, C23, C24, C28, C29, C31, C32, C33), while peer review focuses on the main claim validation (C3, C4, C23, C24, C28) and includes behavioral diversity claims (C38, C39, C45, C49). Both evaluations are SUPPORTED with high confidence.

OpenEval R2 addresses behavioral diversity and temporal dynamics (C38-C49) showing broader/prolonged epidermis-evoked responses. Peer R1 partially overlaps (C38, C39, C45, C49) as part of overall evidence for epidermal activation of sensory neurons. Both are SUPPORTED, though OpenEval provides more detailed analysis of behavioral quantification.

Both address calcium imaging evidence for epidermis-neuron coupling. OpenEval R3 focuses on neuronal activation and tetanus toxin experiments (C50-C54, C58), while peer R2 accepts calcium imaging findings (C50-C52, C58, C130) as complementary to behavioral studies. Both evaluations are SUPPORTED without challenge.

Both address tetanus toxin experiments demonstrating requirement for neuronal output. OpenEval R3 includes broader calcium imaging context (C50-C54, C58), while peer R3 specifically validates tetanus toxin results (C53, C54, C131). Both are SUPPORTED as part of epidermis-neuron coupling evidence.

Perfect alignment on synergistic effects of combined epidermis-nociceptor stimulation (C59-C66). Both evaluations are SUPPORTED, with OpenEval emphasizing quantitative measurements and statistical significance, while peer review accepts findings as convincing evidence for epidermal cell role in nociceptive activation.

Both strongly support sensitization findings. OpenEval R5 focuses on time course quantification and specificity (C67-C71), while peer R5 includes broader context (C7, C8, C67-C71, C110) and treats this as a key advance in mechanosensation understanding. Both evaluations are SUPPORTED.

Strong agreement on intrinsic mechanosensitivity of epidermal cells. Both evaluations are SUPPORTED. OpenEval R6 emphasizes dose-dependent responses and multiple stimulus modalities (C5, C74-C81), while peer R6 confirms the main claim with similar claim coverage (C5, C74-C76, C80, C81).

Both strongly support Stim/Orai mechanism with convergent evidence. OpenEval R7 details genetic, pharmacological, and imaging approaches (C6, C83, C87-C96), while peer R7 emphasizes novelty and significance (C6, C83, C89-C91, C95, C116, C119, C154). Both are SUPPORTED and treat this as a major discovery.

Partial overlap on SOCE mechanism. OpenEval R7 includes pharmacological and zero-calcium experiments (C87, C88, C92-C94) as part of comprehensive Stim/Orai evidence. Peer R8 rates these claims as UNCERTAIN, noting unresolved questions about how mechanical stimulation triggers ER calcium release, despite accepting that both components contribute.

Perfect alignment on human keratinocyte data (C97-C99). Both evaluations are SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes translational relevance with species-specific differences in mechanosensitivity thresholds, while peer review highlights conservation across species as supporting broader significance.

Perfect alignment on gain-of-function experiments (C100, C101). Both evaluations are SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes these complement loss-of-function data and are consistent with Orai channel properties, while peer review accepts them as part of thorough genetic analyses with appropriate controls.

Both address vesicular release in sensitization. OpenEval R10 is SUPPORTED with note about unidentified mediators (C103-C105, C132), while peer R11 is UNCERTAIN, raising concerns about reconciling SOCE kinetics with vesicular release requirements. Agreement on experimental observation but divergence on mechanistic interpretation.

Minimal overlap. OpenEval R10 addresses shibirets experiments (C103-C105, C132), while peer R12 accepts the overall epidermis-as-primary-sensor model (C105, C72, C9, C10, C108, C109). Both are SUPPORTED but address different aspects of the work.

Both address RNA-seq data from epidermal cells. OpenEval R11 focuses on absence of neurotransmitter biosynthesis genes but presence of vesicular machinery (C106, C107), while peer R14 accepts this molecular characterization (C82, C106, C107) as thorough genetic analysis. Both are SUPPORTED.

Both address RNA-seq expression data. OpenEval R12 focuses on ion channel expression (C82) as foundation for screening, while peer R14 accepts broader RNA-seq characterization (C82, C106, C107). Both are SUPPORTED as descriptive molecular evidence.

Both address morphometric control experiments. OpenEval R14 emphasizes ruling out developmental effects on nociceptor structure (C25), while peer R13 accepts these controls (C25, C33) as addressing potential confounds. Both are SUPPORTED.

Both address high-level conclusions about epidermal cells as primary mechanosensors. OpenEval R16 synthesizes multiple experimental findings (C9, C10, C72, C108-C110, C119), while peer R12 accepts the overall model (C72, C9, C10, C108, C109) as significant advance. Both are SUPPORTED.
